common_mistakes: Dusting the coating on long before frying, so it absorbs moisture and fries up soggy instead of crisp.
Flipping pan-fried chicken again and again, when the skin needs one long, undisturbed turn against the pan.
Frying whole dense items like potatoes at the standard 170 degrees, so the outside finishes long before the center.
Skipping the rest between the two fries, which is when carryover heat finishes the center and sets up the crisp second fry.
Stirring stew ingredients constantly as they brown, so they steam in their own juices and never develop the crust that gives the broth its depth.
Flipping skewers again and again on the grill, which tears the meat, leaks its juices and leaves it dry.
core_principles: 170 degrees Celsius is the standard frying temperature in the source recipes, but it is a starting point, not a law.
Dense, whole items go lower and slower: whole new potatoes fry at 160 degrees for about 10 minutes so the center cooks through.
Double-frying separates the jobs: the first fry cooks the inside, a 2-minute rest lets carryover heat finish it, and the second fry crisps the crust.
Coating is a last-second decision: katakuriko goes on right before the food enters the oil, so it stays dry and fries crisp.
Skin gets its own schedule: about 70 percent of the cooking time goes to the skin side, with pressure, so it turns crisp while the flesh stays plump.

Searing is a stage of simmering, not a separate technique: meat and vegetables destined for a stew are first left undisturbed in the pan until browned, which seals in umami and lends the broth a roasted depth.
High heat is a tool in itself, not just a faster low heat: a rolled omelet is cooked over strong heat from start to finish so the steam puffs its layers up before the moisture can escape.

hook_questions: Why do Japanese chefs fry the same chicken twice?

What happens in the one second after smoking oil hits raw spices?
key_facts: 170 degrees Celsius is the working temperature across the source recipes: chicken katsu, chicken nanban, tatsuta-age, fried horse mackerel, fried mackerel and eggplant all fry at 170 degrees.

Chicken katsu is double-fried: 5 minutes at 170 degrees, a 2-minute rest out of the oil, then back into 170-degree oil for 3 more minutes, so the crust turns crisp while the inside finishes juicy on carryover heat.
Whole skin-on new potatoes are fried lower and slower, at 160 degrees for about 10 minutes, so the heat reaches the center.
Eggplant for agebitashi is flash-fried only 1 to 2 minutes at 170 degrees, just until softened, then drained and put straight into the sauce.
Katakuriko is dusted on immediately before frying; coating applied at the last moment is a pro rule for a crisp finish.
In chicken-breast nanban, the skin is separated from the meat and fried on its own until crisp, rather than being fried attached.

For pan-fried chicken, about 70 percent of the total cooking time, roughly 7 to 8 minutes, is spent on the skin side pressed down with a spatula; the chicken is flipped only once, then cooked 3 to 4 minutes on the flesh side.
Vegetables for agebitashi fry about 3 minutes each at 170 degrees and go into the cooled dipping sauce immediately.
Nikujaga is built in two searing stages: the pork belly is browned first and removed, and the potatoes, onions and carrots are then browned in the rendered pork fat before any liquid is added.
Ground meat for a simmered sauce is stir-fried until it turns properly crumbly and lightly browned; undercooked mince keeps a gamy smell that clouds the whole sauce.
A rolled omelet never sees low heat: the pan stays hot the whole time, and each new layer of egg is lifted and rolled quickly so the steam keeps the omelet soft and puffed.
Oil heated until it just begins to smoke, poured directly over raw chili and Sichuan pepper resting on salted cabbage, blooms their aroma in a single second and carries it into every leaf.

Skewered yakitori is packed tight on the skewer with no gaps between pieces, grilled skin-side first when there is skin, and flipped only once, because gaps scorch and repeated flipping leaks the juices.
Thickness sets the frying time at 170 degrees: thin horse mackerel fillets for tatsuta-age need only about 2 minutes in the oil, against 5 minutes for a breaded chicken cutlet.
Hamburg steaks are seared on both sides first, then finished under a lid with a splash of sake for about 5 minutes over low heat, steaming the centers done without drying them out.

practical_steps: Set your oil to 170 degrees Celsius as the default for cutlets, karaage-style chicken and vegetables.
For breaded chicken, fry 5 minutes, rest it 2 minutes out of the oil, then fry 3 minutes more for the crisp finish.
Drop to 160 degrees and give whole potatoes about 10 minutes so the centers cook through.
Dust potato starch onto food at the very last moment before it enters the oil.
Give chicken skin its own time: press it against the pan for most of the cooking and flip only once.
When browning ingredients for a stew, put them in the pan and wait: let a crust form before you move them, and brown meat and vegetables in stages rather than all at once.
Finish a cabbage salad the dramatic way: heat oil until it smokes, then pour it over the chili and pepper sitting on top so the aroma blooms at the table.
Pack skewers tightly with no gaps and commit to a single flip, skin side down first.
Match your frying time to thickness at 170 degrees: about 2 minutes for thin fish fillets, longer for anything with real depth.

theme: Japanese frying is temperature discipline: 170 degrees as the standard, 160 for dense whole items, a rest between two fries, and skin that gets most of the cooking time.
viewer_takeaways: 170 degrees Celsius is the anchor temperature, and knowing when to break from it is the real skill.
The rest between two fries is where the center finishes and the crust gets ready to crisp.
Skin, coating and size each change the plan: give each one the time the oil temperature alone cannot.
Heat control is mostly patience: leave food alone to brown, flip it once, and let the right temperature do the work.
